title: First March tests
summary: Start with the shortest March tests and add operations one at a time. Each addition makes the test catch a new fault model. You will watch a fault escape one test and get caught by the next.
objectives: Write MATS, MATS+, MATS++ and March X and state their length.
Explain which fault model each added operation catches.
Follow a March test on a faulty memory and decide pass or fail.
Show why March X detects inversion coupling faults in both aggressor positions.

subsections.title: MATS, MATS+, MATS++ and March X

blocks.md: **MATS** (Modified Algorithmic Test Sequence) is the shortest useful March test. The others grow from it, one step at a time:

tabs.label: MATS — 4N
tabs.md:
**{⇕(w0); ⇕(r0, w1); ⇕(r1)}**

Every cell is read as 0 and as 1, so all **stuck-at faults** are found. The address order is free (⇕), so the AF condition of Topic 6 is not met: some **address-decoder faults escape**.

tabs.label: MATS+ — 5N
tabs.md:
**{⇕(w0); ⇑(r0, w1); ⇓(r1, w0)}**

One extra operation, and fixed directions: ⇑(r0 … w1) and ⇓(r1 … w0) are exactly the **AF condition**. MATS+ detects all **stuck-at and address-decoder faults**.

tabs.label: MATS++ — 6N
tabs.md:
**{⇕(w0); ⇑(r0, w1); ⇓(r1, w0, r0)}**

The last w0 makes a 1 → 0 transition — but in MATS+ nobody reads it. The added **r0** does. MATS++ adds all **transition faults**.

tabs.label: March X — 6N
tabs.md:
**{⇕(w0); ⇑(r0, w1); ⇓(r1, w0); ⇕(r0)}**

The final read moves into its own element. Same length as MATS++, but now *every* cell is read after *all* cells have made their last transition. March X adds all **inversion coupling faults (CFin)**.

subsections.title: Watch a fault escape — and get caught

blocks.md: Cell 2 of a 4-cell memory has a **transition fault ↓**: it can go 0 → 1, but not 1 → 0. Run MATS+ and MATS++ on it:

steps.title: ⇕(w0)
steps.md: All cells start at 0 — cell 2 included.

steps.title: ⇑(r0, w1)
steps.md: Every read returns 0 ✓. Every w1 works: the fault does not block the 0 → 1 transition.

steps.title: ⇓(r1, w0)
steps.md: Every read returns 1 ✓. Then w0 — but cell 2 **cannot** go back to 0. MATS+ ends here. No read was wrong: **PASS — the faulty memory escapes.**

steps.title: ⇓(r1, w0, r0)
steps.md: MATS++ reads every cell right after writing 0. Cell 2 returns **1 ✗** → **FAIL**. The fault is detected.

blocks.title: The rule behind it
blocks.md: A fault only counts as detected when a **read returns a wrong value**. Every operation that can trigger a fault — a transition, an aggressor write — must be **followed later by a read** of the cell it can damage.

A CFin ⟨↑;↕⟩ or ⟨↓;↕⟩ can have the aggressor **below** the victim (a < v) or **above** it (a > v). A test must catch all four cases. March X has the elements M0 ⇕(w0), M1 ⇑(r0, w1), M2 ⇓(r1, w0), M3 ⇕(r0):

rows: M1 goes up: a is written 1 before v is visited, v flips to 1; then M1 reads v expecting 0
M1 writes v = 1 first, then a rises and flips v to 0; M2 goes down and reads v expecting 1
M2 goes down: v becomes 0 first, then a falls and flips v to 1; M3 reads v expecting 0
M2 goes down: a falls before v is visited and flips v to 0; M2 then reads v expecting 1
blocks.caption: All four CFin cases are detected by March X

blocks.title: Both directions do the work
blocks.md: Going **up**, aggressors below the victim act *before* the victim is read. Going **down**, aggressors above it do. That is why March tests always contain ⇑ **and** ⇓ elements.

blocks.prompt: Practice: which is the shortest test of this topic that detects all faults of each model?

questions.text: Why does MATS+ detect all address-decoder faults, while MATS does not?
options: MATS+ fixes the directions so that it contains ⇑(r0 … w1) and ⇓(r1 … w0).
MATS+ reads every cell three times.

questions.text: A cell cannot go from 1 to 0. Why does MATS+ miss this fault?
options: The last w0 fails, but no read of that cell follows it.
MATS+ only reads in the up direction.
Transition faults cannot be detected by March tests.

questions.text: A fault is detected only when a read returns a value different from the expected one.
In March X, a CFin ⟨↑;↕⟩ with the aggressor **below** the victim is detected in which element?
Match the test to its length.
